background.definition: Hypospadias is a congenital anomaly of the penis in which the urethral meatus is found in an abnormal ventral location.

list.listitem: One in 200 to 1 in 300 live births.
The incidence has reportedly doubled since the 1960s, although discrepancies in reporting may account for some of the increase.

A similar increase in incidence was found in a Swedish population-based study from approximately 4.5 per 1,000 live-born boys until 1990 to 8 per 1,000 boys during the following decade. Changes in risk factors, including small for gestational age (OR 4.34), as a twin (OR 1.8), as a result of in vitro fertilization (OR 1.15), or with parents from Asia (OR 1.45) or continental Europe (OR 1.41), did not explain the increased incidence.
Anterior, middle, and posterior hypospadias account for 65%, 15%, and 20% of cases, respectively.

The prevalence varies worldwide from 0.6/10,000 in Malaysia to 464/10,000 in Denmark. The mean in North America is 34.2/10,000 live-born boys. There is a trend towards increasing prevalence that is not clearly understood but may be attributed to a combination of social factors as well as better diagnosis and treatment.
Hypospadias is the second most common congenital defect in males.
The cause is not completely understood and likely multifactorial.

Hypospadias is thought to be related to a genetic predisposition with several different transcription and growth factors implicated. Seven percent of cases have a first-, second-, or third-degree relative with hypospadias.
Exposure to endocrine disrupters, including diethylstilbestrol and pesticides, is associated with increased risk.
The risk factors shown in the table below suggest that placental health may play a role.
Abnormal urethral development.
Phallus development usually occurs between 8 weeks and 12 weeks' gestation from the previously undifferentiated external genitalia.
This process includes tubularization of the urethra, which occurs in a proximal to distal fashion.
Interruption leads to a ventral urethral opening at the site of cessation of tubularization.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Possibly maternal exposure to some pesticides

list.listitem: The diagnosis relies on the physical examination at the time of the newborn examination or at circumcision.
The hypospadias may be anterior or posterior, and may be associated with chordee, or ventral penile curvature, and/or abnormal ventral foreskin.

The hypospadias may be anterior (on the glans, corona, or anterior penile shaft), middle (mid-penile shaft), or posterior (posterior penile shaft, scrotum, or even the perineum in the most severe cases). It may be associated with chordee, or ventral penile curvature, and/or abnormal ventral foreskin.
In isolated hypospadias, the diagnosis is made by physical examination alone.
When associated with cryptorchidism, karyotype analysis should be performed to evaluate the possibility of intersexuality.
Karyotype analysis is only indicated if intersexuality is a concern.
Hypospadias is typically diagnosed on routine newborn examination.
Diagnostic testing is not typically indicated.
In cases of proximal hypospadias, ultrasound of the urinary tract may be warranted to ensure no other malformations.

Circumcision has traditionally been delayed, and patients referred for surgical correction to a pediatric urologist. There is some debate about the need to interrupt a parental-requested circumcision for newborns with distal hypospadias and an intact prepuce.
The surgeon should discuss whether or not to maintain the foreskin following surgical repair, especially for distal hypospadias, as this is also an area of debate.
Surgical repair is the only treatment; therefore, the patient should be referred to a urologist.
Since foreskin may be used in repair, circumcision should be deferred.
Surgical repair is recommended between 6 and 18 months of life. Timing depends on parent preference as well as severity of the abnormality.

There are multiple reasons to consider treatment, although it is not required. The reasons include spraying of urine, inability to urinate standing, difficulties with intercourse due to penile curvature, fertility issues and patient satisfaction with the appearace of the penis.
The role of preoperative testosterone on operative outcomes after proximal hypospadias repair remains unclear.
A 2023 retrospective cohort of more than 350 infant hypospadias repairs found no change in outcomes with 0, 1, 2, or 3 preoperative injections of testosterone.
Surgical repair is the only treatment.
Repair should take 6 to 18 months of age in an otherwise healthy child.
There are more than 250 described procedures.
Repair should include orthoplasty (penile straightening), urethroplasty, meatoplasty and glanuloplasty, scrotoplasty, and skin coverage.
Proximal defect repair is more technically complex and associated with more complications compared with distal defect repair.

Goals specifically for proximal hypospadias repair are related to long-term quality of life issues for patients. These include voiding with normal flow, obtaining satisfactory sexual function, and improved cosmetic appearance with a slit-like meatus.

If hypospadias is suspected, circumcision should not be performed as the foreskin may be utilized in repair; if the foreskin has been cut prior to discovery of hypospadias, the procedure should be terminated, and referral made.
Authors of a case series of infants with unrecognized glandular hypospadias, however, found similar outcomes regardless of whether circumcision was completed or aborted.
Scoring systems have been developed to standardize severity assessment of hypospadias preoperatively and outcomes postoperatively. There is no agreement on the best scoring algorithm.
Routine antimicrobial prophylaxis reduces the rate of perioperative infection, but the rate is low (<3%) and routine prophylaxis may not be warranted.
Patients with hypospadias should always be referred to a urologist for evaluation.
There are few studies of the long-term prognosis following hypospadias repair, and the results have been inconsistent.

In a 1-year post-surgery follow-up study of 100 parents, decisional regret was identified in 116 parents, which was mild in 41.4% and moderate to severe in 8.6%. Factors associated with regret included surgical complications, parental desire to avoid circumcision (foreskin can be preserved if desired), and initial decisional conflict level.
Surgical complications following repair of distal hypospadias include urethral breakdown or fistula (about 8%), uncommonly phimosis (about 1%) and rare preputial (foreskin) fistulas and breakdowns.

In another case series of distal hypospadias repair in 1,140 patients operated on by a single surgeon, complications developed in 124 of 883 primary repairs (14%) and 85 of 257 reoperations (33%). Complications following reoperation included 8 fistulas, 5 glans dehiscences and 3 meatal stenosis. Complication rates were similar for the 69 adult and pre-pubertal patients.
Following penile and bulbar substitution urethroplasty in a retrospective cohort of 359 patients, 73.8% were successful at a median follow-up of 118 months.
